result: Natural variation in C. elegans egg retention was characterized across 316 wild strains, revealing three phenotypic classes: Class I (weak retention, <10 eggs, 15%), Class II (canonical retention, 10-25 eggs, 81%), and Class III (strong retention, >25 eggs, 4%), with several Class III strains exhibiting internal hatching.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are well-supported by quantitative data from 316 strains with clear sample sizes and percentages. The classification system is empirically defined and supported by Figure 1A-C showing the distribution of egg retention phenotypes. The observation of internal hatching in Class III strains is documented in source data.

result: No obvious relationships were found between egg retention and geographical/climatic parameters or substrate type, with strains from all three classes distributed globally and co-occurring in the same localities. A majority of Class III strains (11/14) were isolated in Europe.
evaluation: Claims C6-C9 are supported by statistical analyses (Spearman correlations, p>0.05) and geographic distribution data. The lack of correlation with ecological parameters is appropriately qualified as 'no obvious evidence,' acknowledging potential limitations. The European bias in Class III strains is noted with appropriate caution about sampling bias.

result: GWA mapping identified a single QTL on chromosome III (1.48 Mb) explaining 24% of phenotypic variance in mean egg retention, plus two additional QTL on chromosomes II and IV for variance. Five genes with known egg-laying roles were found in the chromosome III QTL, but no obvious candidate polymorphisms were detected.
evaluation: Claims C10-C15 are supported by GWA mapping results shown in Figure 2A-B and Table 1. The identification of QTLs is methodologically sound, though the 24% variance explained suggests substantial additional genetic factors. The failure to identify obvious candidate polymorphisms (C13) is appropriately reported as a negative result.

result: Natural variation in C. elegans egg retention is polygenic, influenced by both common variants (detected by GWA) and rare variants including KCNL-1 V530L, explaining extreme phenotypic divergence.
evaluation: Claims C16, C21, C101, C107 are well-supported by the combined evidence from GWA mapping (detecting common variants) and identification of the rare KCNL-1 V530L variant. The inference of polygenic architecture is reasonable given the phenotypic distribution, multiple QTLs, and the fact that only 24% of variance is explained by the major QTL.

result: Four strains carry the KCNL-1 V530L variant that strongly reduces egg-laying activity, likely derived from a single mutational event based on haplotype analysis. Ten additional Class III strains without this variant must have alternative genetic causes for strong egg retention.
evaluation: Claims C17-C20 are supported by genetic data and haplotype analysis (Figure 2C). The single origin of KCNL-1 V530L is well-supported by local haplotype analysis. The inference that other Class III strains must have alternative genetic variants (C20) is logically sound given their phenotype without the known variant.

result: Temporal dynamics of egg number in utero varied strongly across the reproductive span in 15 focal strains, with increased egg retention linked to prolonged intra-uterine embryonic development. Class III strains contained more advanced embryonic stages, and internal hatching occurred consistently in the six strains with highest retention.
evaluation: Claims C22-C26 are well-supported by data in Figure 3C-E showing temporal progression and embryonic age distribution. The link between egg retention and prolonged embryonic development is directly demonstrated. Sample sizes are adequate (N=28-96 per strain per timepoint for most measurements).

result: Both egg and body size showed significant differences across the 15 focal strains with a trend for correlation between them, but neither correlated with mean egg retention, suggesting egg retention capacity is not simply a function of body or egg size.
evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-F. The statistical analyses appropriately distinguish between significant differences in size measurements and lack of correlation with egg retention. The inference that retention is not simply size-dependent (C29) is reasonable given the data.

result: Egg-laying activity was highly dynamic, peaking at mid-L4 +24-30 hr, with Class III strains showing shortened time windows. The number of intervals with egg laying varied significantly between strains and classes, with Class I showing increased and Class IIIB showing reduced intervals. The N2 strain expelled significantly more eggs per interval than all other strains.
evaluation: Claims C30-C37 are well-supported by behavioral data in Figures 4 and 5. The scan-sampling method (5-min intervals over 3 hr) is appropriate for detecting differences in egg-laying patterns, though it cannot resolve fine temporal structure of active phases. Statistical analyses (Two-Way ANOVA) are appropriate with adequate sample sizes (N=17-18 per strain).

result: Class II hermaphrodites laid their first egg after accumulating ~5-10 eggs in utero (~1-2 hr after fertilization), while Class I and III strains showed significantly advanced and delayed first egg-laying events, respectively, with corresponding differences in egg accumulation.
evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by data in Figure 6A-B showing timing and egg accumulation at first egg-laying. The measurements are consistent with previous reports for N2 (Ravi et al., 2018). Sample sizes are adequate (N=16-22 per strain) and statistical differences are demonstrated.

result: Exposure to 25 mM serotonin consistently increased egg laying in Class I and II strains, but responses were highly variable in Class III strains. Serotonin stimulated egg laying in most Class IIIA strains except JU2829 (where it inhibited), induced stronger response in ED3005, and had no effect or inhibited egg laying in Class IIIB strains.
evaluation: Claims C40-C44 are well-supported by pharmacological data in Figure 7B. The experimental design is appropriate with parallel controls and adequate replication (N=11-24 replicates per strain). Statistical analyses (Align Rank Transform ANOVA) are appropriate for the data. The variable responses across strains are clearly demonstrated.

result: Fluoxetine and imipramine strongly stimulated egg-laying activity in all 15 focal strains with only slight quantitative differences in drug sensitivity. Both drugs stimulated egg laying even in Class IIIB strains and JU2829 where serotonin had no effect or inhibited egg laying.
evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by data in Figure 7B showing consistent stimulatory effects across all strains. The observation that these drugs work even when serotonin doesn't is important for understanding the neuromodulatory architecture. Statistical analyses confirm significant effects with appropriate controls.

result: CRISPR-engineered manipulation of KCNL-1 demonstrated that the V530L variant is sufficient to abrogate positive but not negative serotonin inputs. Introducing the variant into JU1200 recapitulated the inhibitory serotonin response, while reverting it in JU751 restored normal responses. Both fluoxetine and imipramine stimulated egg laying regardless of KCNL-1 genotype.
evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are strongly supported by reciprocal CRISPR experiments shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The genetic manipulation provides causal evidence that KCNL-1 V530L is sufficient to explain the altered serotonin response. The experimental design with reciprocal edits in two genetic backgrounds is rigorous.

result: Introduction of mod-5(n822) loss-of-function mutation increased basal egg-laying activity in most but not all strains, with genotype-dependent effects. Several strains showed no significant increase, and the effect was quantitatively different within the same phenotypic class. At high serotonin (25 mM), mod-5(n822) did not further increase egg laying except in ED3005.
evaluation: Claims C51-C54 are supported by data in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A. The CRISPR-mediated introduction of mod-5(n822) into 10 strains provides strong evidence for genotype-dependent effects. Statistical analyses (Align Rank Transform ANOVA) appropriately detect the significant interaction between genetic background and mod-5 genotype.

result: Exposure to lower serotonin concentrations revealed significant strain differences in sensitivity that were contingent on mod-5(lf) presence. Low serotonin strongly stimulated egg laying in Class I strains and ED3005, amplified by mod-5(lf), while Class II strains showed only marginal increases. This demonstrates natural variation in genetic architecture affecting neuromodulatory sensitivity.
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are well-supported by data in Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, and Table 3. The significant three-way interaction (genetic background × mod-5 × serotonin concentration) provides strong evidence for epistasis. The experimental design with multiple serotonin concentrations effectively reveals genotype-dependent sensitivity differences.

result: Strains with stronger egg retention showed reduced lifetime self-fertility and survival, with strongest reductions in Class IIIB strains. Class III strains showed frequent internal hatching with premature maternal death, while Class I and II strains showed absent or rare internal hatching at the end of reproduction.
evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are supported by data in Figures 9A-C and 10A-C. The correlations between egg retention and reduced fitness are clearly demonstrated. Sample sizes are adequate (N=28-30 for fertility, N=90-102 for survival). The temporal progression of internal hatching is well-documented.

result: Multiple Class III strains had self-sperm remaining at internal hatching, with JU2593 showing total sperm greatly exceeding lifetime progeny. Internally hatched larvae caused physical damage to maternal tissues and scattered sperm away from spermathecae, likely reducing fertilization efficacy as evidenced by unfertilized oocytes.
evaluation: Claims C62-C65 are supported by DAPI staining data in Figure 11 and Figure 11—figure supplement 1. The co-occurrence of sperm and internally hatched larvae is clearly demonstrated. The observations of physical damage and scattered sperm provide mechanistic insight into reduced fertility. Sample sizes are adequate (N=46-175 for sperm counts).

result: Strong egg retention correlates with reduced self-fertility and maternal survival, with Class IIIB strains showing the most drastic reductions and using only a fraction of available self-sperm. In contrast, Class IIIA strains (ED3005, JU440, NIC1786) showed internal hatching mainly after reproduction ceased, suggesting limited detrimental fitness effects.
evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by data in Figures 9C, 10B-C, and 11. The correlations are clearly demonstrated, and the distinction between Class IIIA and IIIB in timing of internal hatching relative to reproduction is important. The inference about limited fitness effects in some Class IIIA strains (C69) is reasonable given the timing data.

result: Strong egg retention reflects prolonged intra-uterine development, resulting in laying of advanced-stage embryos. Class III strains laid embryos with hundreds of cells (sometimes close to hatching), hatched 2-5 hours earlier, and many reached maturity 2-6 hours earlier than Class I/II strains, benefiting from shorter developmental time from laying to maturity.
evaluation: Claims C70-C74 are well-supported by data in Figures 3D, 12A-C. The age distribution of embryos in laid eggs is clearly documented. The measurements of hatching time and egg-to-adult developmental time are appropriate with adequate sample sizes (N=30-318 eggs per strain). The inference about competitive advantage (C74) is reasonable given the data.

result: Competition experiments showed that the KCNL-1 V530L variant performed significantly better against a GFP-tester strain, and JU751 reached higher adult population sizes than strains from the same habitat at food exhaustion. This provides preliminary evidence that laying advanced-stage embryos may enhance competitive ability in resource-limited environments.
evaluation: Claims C75-C78 are supported by competition data in Figure 12D-E. The experimental design is appropriate with adequate replication (N=10 per genotype). However, the authors appropriately qualify this as 'preliminary evidence' (C78) given the focus on a single genetic background. The inference about competitive advantage is reasonable but would benefit from additional genetic backgrounds.

result: Previous studies showed increased egg-to-adult developmental time is disadvantageous for C. elegans population growth in resource-limited conditions. Combined with evidence from insects, this indicates maternal features accelerating offspring development after oviposition can confer fitness benefits in ephemeral habitats.
evaluation: Claims C79-C80 appropriately cite previous work (Hodgkin and Barnes, 1991; Barker, 1992; Cutter, 2004; Bakker, 1961; Mueller and Bitner, 2015; Horváth and Kalinka, 2018) to contextualize the current findings. The inference about fitness benefits (C80) is reasonable given the combined evidence from multiple taxa.

result: Eggs inside mothers exhibited significantly higher survival than eggs ex utero when exposed to high concentrations of ethanol and acetic acid, particularly for acetic acid. Increased egg retention resulted in higher numbers of surviving offspring per mother. Larvae in utero were also efficiently protected.
evaluation: Claims C81-C85 are well-supported by data in Figures 13A-B and 14A-C. The experimental design comparing ex utero vs in utero exposure is appropriate. Statistical analyses show significant differences. Sample sizes are adequate (N=5-10 replicates per treatment). The protection of both eggs and larvae is clearly demonstrated.

result: Offspring from stress-exposed eggs ex utero showed reduced fertility (osmotic stress) or delayed reproductive maturity (mild acetic acid) compared to eggs in utero. Larvae in utero at stress exposure were protected and produced as many offspring as controls.
evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by data in Figure 15B-D. The experimental design tracking offspring fitness is appropriate. The distinction between effects on fertility vs developmental timing is important. Sample sizes are adequate (N=15-19 per treatment). The protection of larvae in utero is clearly demonstrated.

result: Constitutively strong egg retention can enhance maternal protection of offspring by protecting more eggs in utero during sudden environmental perturbations and reducing external exposure time of the immobile embryonic stage. The degree of egg retention alters the interplay of antagonistic effects on maternal versus offspring fitness.
evaluation: Claims C89-C91 are well-supported by the combined results from stress experiments (Figures 13-15). The inference about enhanced protection (C89) is strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence. The inference about reduced exposure time (C90) is logical. The conclusion about antagonistic effects (C91) appropriately synthesizes the fitness cost and benefit data.

result: Strong egg retention reduces maternal survival and reproduction, but prolonged intra-uterine development may benefit offspring through improved competitive ability and protection against environmental insults. Variable egg retention may reflect genetic differences in adjustment of an intergenerational fitness trade-off.
evaluation: Claims C92-C95 appropriately synthesize the major findings on costs (Figures 9-10) and benefits (Figures 12-15) of egg retention. The inference about an intergenerational fitness trade-off (C95) is well-supported by the combined evidence, though the authors appropriately use 'may reflect' to acknowledge this is an interpretation.

result: In extreme cases, C. elegans strains exhibit partial viviparity associated with reduced maternal reproduction and survival. This aligns with reports across diverse taxa showing transitions towards viviparity incur maternal fitness costs.
evaluation: Claims C96-C97 are supported by the data on Class III strains and appropriately contextualized with literature across diverse taxa (Avise, 2013; Blackburn, 2015; Kalinka, 2015; Ostrovsky et al., 2016; Horváth and Kalinka, 2018; Whittington et al., 2022). The comparison to other taxa is appropriate and strengthens the interpretation.

result: Given the nearly exclusive selfing mode of C. elegans reproduction, there is expected to be little genetic disparity between mothers and offspring, indicating reduced opportunities for intergenerational conflict. Observed differences in egg retention likely reflect properties of clonally propagating genotypes adapted to distinct ecological niches.
evaluation: Claims C98-C99 appropriately draw on established knowledge about C. elegans reproductive mode (Barrière and Félix, 2005; Lee et al., 2021) to interpret the findings. The inference about reduced intergenerational conflict (C98) is logical given the selfing mode. The speculation about ecological adaptation (C99) is reasonable but appropriately qualified as 'predicted' and 'likely.'

result: Summary of main findings: C. elegans exhibits quantitative variation in egg retention with rare extreme phenotypes. Strain differences are largely explained by differences in egg-laying behavior mapping to genetic differences in neuromodulator sensitivity. Strong egg retention negatively impacts maternal fitness but may benefit offspring, reflecting variation in a trade-off between maternal and offspring fitness.
evaluation: Claims C100, C102-C106 appropriately summarize the major findings of the study. These summary claims are well-supported by the collective evidence from all experiments. The synthesis of behavioral, genetic, and fitness data provides a comprehensive picture of natural variation in egg retention.

result: Variation in reproductive processes (sperm production, ovulation rates) contributes to egg retention variation, but there is clear evidence for natural variation in egg-laying behavior and neuromodulatory processes. Changes in muscle-directed signaling in response to egg accumulation are likely key factors driving evolution of egg retention.
evaluation: Claims C109 and C115 appropriately acknowledge multiple contributing factors to egg retention. The inference about muscle-directed signaling (C115) is supported by data in Figure 6B and is consistent with recent literature on stretch-dependent mechanisms (Collins et al., 2016; Ravi et al., 2018; Ravi et al., 2021; Medrano and Collins, 2023).

result: Background on C. elegans egg-laying circuit: Decades of research identified dozens of genes affecting egg-laying activity, including ion channels, G-protein signaling components, and sensory processing genes. Recent research uncovered muscle-directed stretch-sensing mechanisms that can trigger egg laying independently of synaptic transmission.
evaluation: Claims C110-C114 appropriately summarize established knowledge about the C. elegans egg-laying circuit, drawing on extensive prior literature (Trent et al., 1983; Schafer, 2006; Ringstad and Horvitz, 2008; Fenk and de Bono, 2015; Banerjee et al., 2017; Collins et al., 2016; Ravi et al., 2018; Ravi et al., 2021; Medrano and Collins, 2023). This provides essential context for interpreting the current findings.

result: KCNL-1 V530L is currently the only known natural variant modulating C. elegans egg laying, but other unknown variants must cause strong egg retention in Class IIIA strains. JU2829 might carry a variant with effects like KCNL-1 V530L, while other Class IIIA strains likely have variants with distinct functional effects. Detection of strain variation indicates many different natural variants modulate egg-laying circuitry.
evaluation: Claims C117-C120 appropriately acknowledge current knowledge limitations and make reasonable inferences from the data. The inference that other variants must exist (C118) is logically sound. The speculation about JU2829 (C119) is reasonable given its unique serotonin response. The conclusion about multiple variants (C120) is well-supported by the observed variation.

result: The ecological factors shaping natural variation in egg retention are unknown, with no obvious links to habitat parameters. However, ancestral strains rarely exhibited Class III phenotype, suggesting strong egg retention may have been favored during recent C. elegans expansion into novel microhabitats.
evaluation: Claim C122 is supported by the lack of observed correlations. However, claim C123 is speculative, based on limited data (most Class III strains have swept haplotypes, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and draws on population history literature (Lee et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2021). The inference is plausible but requires more direct evidence linking egg retention to specific ecological factors.

result: Background on C. elegans ecology and plasticity: The typical habitat is highly ephemeral with extreme fluctuations. Egg laying is highly plastic, strongly modulated by diverse environmental factors. Long-term stress exposure leads to strong egg retention and matricidal hatching, which may allow nutrient provisioning of larvae through maternal consumption.
evaluation: Claims C124-C127 appropriately summarize established knowledge about C. elegans ecology and egg-laying plasticity, drawing on extensive prior literature (Frézal and Félix, 2015; Schulenburg and Félix, 2017; Trent, 1982; Aballay et al., 2000; Waggoner et al., 2000; Chen and Caswell-Chen, 2003; Schafer, 2005; Zhang et al., 2008; McMullen et al., 2012; Fenk and de Bono, 2015; Vigne et al., 2021; Chen and Caswell-Chen, 2004). This provides important context for understanding the significance of constitutive variation.

result: The existence of natural variation in C. elegans egg retention provides opportunities to dissect the molecular genetic basis of intraspecific variation, offering insights into evolutionary transitions between ovi- and viviparity. C. elegans allows rapid genetic analysis compared to vertebrate systems. Nematodes show frequent transitions to viviparity, but the genetic changes in C. vivipara remain unexamined.
evaluation: Claims C128-C133 appropriately discuss the significance and future directions of the work. The statements about C. elegans as a model system (C129) are well-supported by established knowledge (Recknagel et al., 2021; Whittington et al., 2022; Evans et al., 2021). The statements about nematode viviparity (C130-C132) appropriately cite relevant literature (Sudhaus, 1976; Ostrovsky et al., 2016; Stevens et al., 2019; Loer and Rivard, 2007).
